dev_notes: src/commands/init.mjs. Flags: --product, --accent, --logo, --agents, --style, --tagline, --prepared-for, --commit-pdfs, --force, --no-gitignore. DEFAULT_CONFIG, DEFAULT_BRAND and COMMITTED_CLIENT_DIR are in src/store.mjs; the categories list is deliberately empty at init. --commit-pdfs only moves output.client_dir out of output.dir, which is the single line added to .gitignore; pdfsAreCommitted() derives the shape from that pair and picks the wording for the agent stanza, .ledger/README.md and `ledger status`.

history.name: Creating a ledger in an existing project
history.description: The command ledger init creates a .ledger directory holding the whole corpus: the product name, the accent colour and the style guide you chose, and version 1 open as the release in progress. Everything the tool needs sits in that one directory, so a Python, Go or Rails repo looks identical to it. Setup also adds the generated documents to .gitignore, because the corpus is the part you commit.

The command ledger init creates a .ledger directory holding the whole corpus: the product name, the accent colour and the style guide you chose, and version 1 open as the release in progress. Everything the tool needs sits in that one directory, so a Python, Go or Rails repo looks identical to it. Setup also settles where the generated documents go. The Markdown docs are build output and are added to .gitignore. The PDF editions for the client are build output too, unless you run ledger init --commit-pdfs, which keeps them in docs/client so every document handed over stays in the repo.

The command ledger init sets up a ledger in an existing project: one directory holding the product name, the accent colour, the style guide you chose, and version 1 open as the release in progress. The generated documents stay out of the repository, unless you choose at setup to keep every client edition in it.
history.how_to_see: In a project with no ledger, run ledger init. It creates the .ledger directory, adds the generated docs to .gitignore, and ends with the next steps: survey the codebase, read and edit the result, commit, then cut the baseline.

events.what: Setup also lists the files that aren't product code, such as tests, lockfiles and CI, and keeps what the last preview saw out of the repository.
events.why: So that ownership starts with only the product's own code to account for, and so that when somebody last looked stays theirs.

events.what: Setup no longer lists the files that aren't product code, and keeps nothing out of the repository but the generated docs.
events.why: The ledger no longer maps code to entries, and nothing remembers the last preview.
